Hook.voiceover: Your marketing team started using an AI writing tool last month. Your HR team is testing a tool that ranks job applicants. Nobody asked the legal team first. So who decided these tools were acceptable, and who will answer for them if something goes wrong?

Explain.voiceover: Hi, and welcome to AI Governance, Privacy and Compliance. That question is exactly what AI governance exists to answer. Before we start, one important point. This course is educational and is not legal advice. For decisions about your own organisation, speak to qualified legal advisers.

slide.title: What AI Governance Is and Why It Matters
slide.body: AI Governance, Privacy and Compliance · Lesson 1 of 14. Footer line: Educational, not legal advice.

Explain.voiceover: So what is AI governance? It is the set of roles, policies, processes and controls that decide how an organisation builds, buys and uses AI. It is not one document, and it is not one team. It connects four areas that are often managed separately: legal compliance, ethics, information security and business risk.

slide.title: AI governance
slide.body: Centre circle: Roles, policies, processes and controls for building, buying and using AI. Four connected boxes around it: Legal compliance · Ethics · Information security · Business risk

Explain.voiceover: Most frameworks, whatever their source, share six building blocks. Roles say who is accountable, who approves and who owns each system. Principles are a short list of commitments, such as fairness and human oversight. The inventory lists every AI system you use, including features inside software you already have.

slide.title: Six building blocks
slide.body: Six tiles in two rows, first three highlighted in turn: 1 Roles (who is accountable, approves, owns) · 2 Principles (short list of commitments) · 3 Inventory (every AI system, bought and built). Tiles 4 to 6 greyed out.

Explain.voiceover: Risk assessment is a repeatable way to judge each system's risks to people and to the organisation. Controls are the measures that reduce risk, such as approval steps, testing, human review and contract terms. And monitoring checks that systems keep working after launch, with a process for incidents and complaints.

slide.title: Six building blocks
slide.body: Same six tiles, now tiles 4 to 6 highlighted in turn: 4 Risk assessment (risks to people and organisation) · 5 Controls (approval, testing, human review, contracts) · 6 Monitoring (after launch, incidents, complaints)

Explain.voiceover: Why does this matter to you? First, AI-specific law, such as the EU AI Act, places duties on organisations according to the risk of each AI use. Second, data protection laws, such as the GDPR and Nigeria's NDPA, already apply whenever AI processes personal data. Third, regulators usually ask one question: can you show what you decided, and why?

slide.title: Why it matters
slide.body: 1. AI-specific law: duties by risk (EU AI Act) · 2. Data protection law applies to AI (GDPR, NDPA) · 3. The key question: can you show what you decided, and why?

Explain.voiceover: Here is a helpful way to picture it. AI governance is the building code and the inspection plan, not the building itself. Engineers still design and build. The code says what standards the building must meet. The inspection plan says who checks it, when, and what happens if a check fails.
Explain.on_screen_text: The code and the inspection plan

Explain.voiceover: Good governance is also proportionate. A spelling assistant does not need the same review as a system that decides who gets a loan. The building blocks help you match your effort to the level of risk.

slide.title: Match effort to risk
slide.body: Left: spelling assistant, light review (one small check icon). Right: loan decision system, full review (stack of check icons). Arrow underneath labelled: effort grows with risk

Demonstrate.voiceover: Let's see this in practice. Farida Haddad is the new compliance manager at a fictional engineering consultancy with offices in Amman and Dublin. She is asked to sort out AI. So she checks the six building blocks, one by one.
Demonstrate.stock_query: compliance manager reviewing documents in office

Demonstrate.voiceover: Roles: nobody is named, and each department chooses its own tools. Principles: the code of conduct does not mention AI. Inventory: a short staff survey finds eleven AI tools in use, and four were bought by individual staff with company cards.

slide.title: Farida's gap check
slide.body: Roles: nobody named (red) · Principles: code of conduct silent on AI (red) · Inventory: 11 AI tools found, 4 bought on company cards (amber)

Demonstrate.voiceover: Risk assessment: there is none, and the records of processing do not mention the AI tools. Controls: one team bans pasting client drawings into public chatbots, but other teams do not. Monitoring: nothing is reviewed after purchase.

slide.title: Farida's gap check
slide.body: Risk assessment: none; records of processing silent on AI (red) · Controls: one team only (amber) · Monitoring: nothing after purchase (red)

Demonstrate.voiceover: Farida does not try to fix everything at once. She proposes an accountable executive, a small review group and a short interim rule, while a full policy is drafted. Her gap list becomes the plan for the next quarter.

slide.title: First steps, not everything
slide.body: Three boxes left to right: Accountable executive → Small review group → Short interim rule. Below: Full policy (in progress). Caption: Gap list = next quarter's plan

Demonstrate.voiceover: One common mistake is to treat AI governance as simply writing an AI policy. A policy is only one control. If nobody owns the inventory, and nobody assesses new tools, the policy has no effect. Start with roles and the inventory, because everything else depends on them.
Demonstrate.on_screen_text: A policy alone is not governance.

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, AI governance is the set of roles, policies, processes and controls that decide how an organisation builds, buys and uses AI. Second, six building blocks appear in most frameworks: roles, principles, inventory, risk assessment, controls and monitoring. Third, governance helps you show what you decided and why.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. AI governance = roles, policies, processes and controls for AI. 2. Six blocks: roles, principles, inventory, risk assessment, controls, monitoring. 3. Governance shows what you decided and why.

CTA.voiceover: Now it is your turn. In the exercise below this video, you will use a free policy template to list the six building blocks, and write one honest sentence on how your own organisation handles each today. Please do not paste confidential information into any AI tool.

slide.title: Your exercise
slide.body: Free policy template · Table: building block | how we handle it today · Mark the largest gap · No confidential data in AI tools · About 20 minutes

CTA.voiceover: By the end of the course, you will draft a governance policy and a risk register for a fictional company, Velmora Tradeways. In the next lesson, we look at the regulatory map: three laws, different jobs. See you there.
